questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the Shine-Dalgarno sequence?
questions.solutionHtml:
strong>of the initiating AUG codon on the mRNA molecule  (near its 5'-end).

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Eukaryotic mRNA possesses Shine-Dalgarno sequence: Only the prokaryotic mRNA possesses the sequence.                                

 

Option C. and Option D. both are incorrect as 16S rRNA component of 30S ribosomal subunit has a nucleotide sequence near its 3'-end that is complementary to all or part of the SD sequence

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a ribosomal binding site in the mRNA of prokaryotes, not eukaryotes. It is located upstream of the start codon and is complementary to a sequence at the 3' end of the 16S rRNA in the 30S small subunit of the ribosome. This complementarity facilitates the binding of mRNA to the ribosome, positioning the start codon in the correct place to initiate translation.

 

Ref: Lippincott 6/ed: p 439.

questions.stem: A research team is examining the regulation of fetal hemoglobin expression and the gene product involved in its down regulation. They have primary tissue cultures from fetal, neonatal, and adult liver and bone marrow, along with a DNA probe for the gene of interest. To determine the gene's expression levels in these tissue culture samples, which method is most appropriate?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: DNA sequencing and Option D: Southern blot: These techniques examine the DNA of the cell and the DNA of all the cells involved is identical.

 

Option C: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): It is used to amplify DNA and cannot determine which tissue culture has expressed the gene being studied. It also amplifies the DNA probe which is necessary for Northern blotting. However, in this case, the DNA probe was supplied in adequate amounts → therefore PCR is not recommended.

 

Educational objective:

 

Northern blotting is the correct method for determining the expression of a specific gene. It measures mRNA levels, which correlate directly with gene expression. This technique involves the separation of RNA by gel electrophoresis, transfer to a membrane, and hybridization with a labelled probe specific to the mRNA of interest.

questions.stem: Which DNA polymerase is primarily responsible for DNA repair in mammalian cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
nbsp;

 

Prokaryotic DNA Polymerase has 3 types: Pol I, Pol II and Pol III.

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Alpha - DNA polymerase alpha is primarily involved in the initiation of DNA replication, particularly the synthesis of short RNA-DNA primers, rather than DNA repair.

 

Option C: Gamma - DNA polymerase gamma is responsible for the replication and repair of mitochondrial DNA, not nuclear DNA repair.

 

Option D: Epsilon - DNA polymerase epsilon is involved in leading-strand synthesis during DNA replication and also plays roles in DNA repair, but DNA polymerase beta is more specifically associated with the base excision repair pathway.

 

Educational Objective:

 

DNA polymerase beta (β) plays a key role in the base excision repair (BER) pathway in mammalian cells, which is crucial for repairing small-scale DNA damage such as single-base lesions. This polymerase fills in the single-nucleotide gap left after the removal of a damaged base, contributing significantly to the maintenance of genomic stability.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e page 383.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following codons with the correct amino acid they code for or their function in this specialized context:
questions.solutionHtml:
nt-size:12.0pt;">Explanation:

 

1. UGA → B) Selenocysteine

  • Normally: A stop codon.
  • Special context: With a specific SECIS element (Selenocysteine Insertion Sequence), UGA is redefined to insert selenocysteine.

Correct match: 1-b

 

2. UAG → A) Pyrrolysine

  • Normally: A stop codon.
  • Special context: In certain bacteria, UAG can code for pyrrolysine, the 22nd amino acid.

Correct match: 2-a

 

3. AUG → D) Methionine

  • Always: The standard start codon and codes for methionine.

Correct match: 3-d

 

4. UCA → C) Serine

  • Always: Codes for serine under the standard genetic code.

Correct match: 4-c

 

Other Options:

  • Option B. 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-b
    UAG does not code for serine; UCA does.
    UCA doesn’t code for selenocysteine.
  • Option C. 1-a, 2-d, 3-b, 4-c
    UGA codes for selenocysteine, not pyrrolysine.
    AUG codes for methionine, not selenocysteine.
  • Option D. 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-d is incorrect

     

Educational Objective:

 

Understand the standard genetic code and recognize exceptions like:

  • UGA coding for selenocysteine in the presence of SECIS.
  • UAG coding for pyrrolysine in some organisms.
  • AUG as the universal start codon for methionine.
  • UCA coding for serine in standard contexts.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with developmental delay and a behavioral history of self-injurious actions, including tongue biting and finger biting to the point of needing bandages, is brought to a pediatric neurologist. Based on the clinical presentation, which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
lsive self-destructive behaviors.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Cystathionine synthase: Deficiency results in homocystinuria, characterized by elevated urinary homocysteine. C/F- failure to thrive and visual problems due to lens displacement.  Also deficiency of methionine synthase, pyridoxine, folate, or vitamin B12 can cause homocystinuria.

 

Option C. Homogentisic acid oxidase: Deficiency results in alkaptonuria. C/F- dark urine and darkening of connective tissue (e.g., ear cartilage may appear bluish).

 

Option D. Hexosaminidase A: Deficiency causes Tay-Sachs disease 🡪 results in the accumulation of GM2 ganglioside. C/F-mental retardation, blindness with cherry-red spot on the macula and muscular weakness.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, a disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HPRT), and its deficiency leads to the overproduction of uric acid and a host of neurological and behavioral abnormalities, including self-mutilation behaviors.

 

Ref: Lippincott 7/e: P 296-297.

questions.stem: Regarding the lactose (lac) operon in bacteria, which of the following statements is accurate?

options.label: C
options.text: Contain regulatory genes, an operator gene, three structural genes and a promoter site

options.label: D
options.text: Contain three structural genes, an operator and regulatory gene

questions.answerText: Contain regulatory genes, an operator gene, three structural genes and a promoter site
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="text-align:justify;"> 

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Contains three structural genes: While true, this option is incomplete as it doesn't mention other critical components of the lac operon.

 

Option B. Contains operator region: This is also correct but incomplete, as the lac operon includes more than just an operator region.

 

Option D. Contains three structural genes, an operator, and a regulatory gene: This option is partially correct but lacks the mention of the promoter site and implies the regulatory gene is part of the operon, whereas it is usually located elsewhere on the chromosome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The lac operon is a well-studied example of a gene regulatory system and includes three structural genes (lacZ, lacY, and lacA) that are involved in lactose metabolism. It also has a promoter site where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription, an operator site where the lac repressor can bind to inhibit transcription, and regulatory genes (such as the lacI gene that codes for the lac repressor protein) that control the operon's expression.

 

Ref: DM Vasudevan 9/e: p 636




DM Vasudevan 9/e: p 636

questions.stem: Which of the following cell types do not have the enzyme telomerase that protects the length of telomeres at the chromosomal ends?
questions.solutionHtml:
. D. Somatic

 

Explanation:

 

Telomerase is an enzyme that adds repetitive nucleotide sequences to the ends of chromosomes (telomeres), thereby preventing their progressive shortening during DNA replication. This is especially important in cells that divide frequently or require long-term proliferative potential.

 

Somatic cells, which constitute the majority of cells in the body (like skin, muscle, and liver cells), lack significant telomerase activity. As a result, with each cell division, telomeres become progressively shorter. Eventually, this leads to cellular senescence or programmed cell death (apoptosis), which is a natural part of aging.

 

In contrast:

  • Germinal (germ) cells have active telomerase to ensure genomic stability is passed on to offspring.
  • Tumor cells often reactivate telomerase, which enables them to escape normal cellular aging and divide indefinitely — a key feature of cancer.
  • Hemopoietic stem cells (in bone marrow) also express telomerase to maintain their replicative capacity and continually replenish blood cells.

Educational Objective:

 

Understand that somatic cells typically lack telomerase, which causes telomere shortening over time and contributes to the natural aging process and cellular lifespan limitation. This contrasts with cell types like germinal, stem, and cancer cells, where telomerase activity supports sustained proliferation.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e page 374.



Harper 30/e page 374.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman at 32 weeks of gestation presents for her routine prenatal visit. She has a history of recurrent folate deficiencies. Her current blood work reveals macrocytic anemia. A deficiency in folate would most likely decrease the production of which of the following compounds?

options.label: A
options.text: The thymine nucleotide required for DNA synthesis

options.label: C
options.text: All of the pyrimidines required for RNA synthesis

questions.answerText: The thymine nucleotide required for DNA synthesis
questions.solutionHtml:
pt;">Explanation:

 

Option B. Creatine phosphate from creatine: The synthesis of creatine phosphate from creatine is not directly related to folate metabolism and is unaffected by folate levels.

 

Option C. All of the pyrimidines required for RNA synthesis: While folate is involved in nucleotide synthesis, its deficiency primarily affects the production of thymine, not all pyrimidines.

 

Option D. Phosphatidylcholine from diacylglycerol and CDP-choline: The synthesis of phosphatidylcholine from diacylglycerol and CDP-choline is a part of lipid metabolism and is not dependent on folate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Folate deficiency affects DNA synthesis, particularly the synthesis of thymine nucleotide. Folate is required for the production of tetrahydrofolate (THF), which acts as a carrier of one-carbon units necessary in various metabolic processes, including the methylation of deoxyuridylic acid (dUMP) to thymidylic acid (dTMP), a precursor of thymine nucleotide.

 

Ref: Lippincott 6/e:  p 303-304.

questions.stem: Among the options listed below, which one is not involved in the post-transcriptional processing of the primary mRNA transcript?
questions.solutionHtml:
ify;">Option A. 7-methylguanosine capping at 5’ end: This is a modification that occurs shortly after the initiation of transcription and is crucial for mRNA stability and ribosome recognition.

 

Option B. Poly-A tail at 3’ end:  The addition of a poly-A tail is another key post-transcriptional modification that increases mRNA stability and aids in its export from the nucleus.

 

Option C. Splicing: Splicing involves the removal of introns and joining of exons to form a continuous coding sequence in mRNA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Post-transcriptional modifications:

 

  1. 7-methylguanosine capping at 5’ end

  2. Addition of a poly-A tail at 3’ end

  3. Removal of introns and joining of Exons called Splicing

  4. Methylations

  5. Alternative RNA Processing

 

Post–translational Modifications

 

  1. Covalent modifications of aminoacyl residues

  2. Gamma carboxylation

  3. Hydroxylation

  4. Methylation

  5. Glycosylation

  6. Zymogen activation.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences represents the correct order of enzyme activity in DNA replication?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA polymerase → protein unwinding enzyme → DNA ligase → DNA Isomerase → Polymerase I

options.label: B
options.text: RNA polymerase → DNA polymerase III → DNA polymerase I → DNA ligase

options.label: C
options.text: RNA polymerase → DNA polymerase III → DNA ligase → exonuclease → DNA polymerase I

options.label: D
options.text: Protein unwinding enzyme → polymerase I → DNA ligase → DNA isomerase → DNA polymerase

questions.answerText: RNA polymerase → DNA polymerase III → DNA polymerase I → DNA ligase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) RNA Polymerase → DNA polymerase III → DNA polymerase I → DNA ligase

 

Option B:

 

  • The correct sequence of enzymes includes Helicase, Primase, DNA Polymerase III, DNA Polymerase I and on lagging strand, DNA ligase.

  • Leading strand - Helicase, Primase, DNA Polymerase III

 

Educational Objective:

 

During DNA replication, RNA polymerase (primase) first lays down an RNA primer. DNA polymerase III then extends the DNA strand by adding nucleotides to the primer. DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA. DNA ligase seals the nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone, completing the replication process.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e page 381.



Harper 30/e page 381.

questions.stem: A teenage boy, self-conscious about his weight, decides to follow a fat-free diet in hopes of improving his physique. After adhering to this dietary regimen for several weeks, he visits a nutritionist for a consultation. Concerned about potential nutritional deficiencies and their impact on lipid metabolism, the nutritionist reviews the boy's diet and decides to assess his body's ability to synthesize various essential lipids that might be affected by his restrictive diet:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Prostaglandins

 

Option B:

 

Prostaglandins are synthesized from essential fatty acids, such as arachidonic acid, which are typically obtained from dietary fats. A fat-free diet could lead to a deficiency in essential fatty acids, impacting the body's ability to synthesize prostaglandins. Prostaglandins play various roles in the body, including inflammation, pain modulation, and regulation of blood flow.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: Cholesterol: The body can synthesize cholesterol endogenously, primarily in the liver, and its synthesis is less likely to be directly affected by a fat-free diet.

 

Option C: Glycolipids: Glycolipids are composed of a carbohydrate and a lipid. While dietary fats influence lipid components, the body can also synthesize these from other sources.

 

Option D: Phospholipids: Phospholipids can be synthesized endogenously from glycerol, fatty acids, and phosphate. The body can adapt to variations in dietary fat intake to maintain phospholipid synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Prostaglandins are synthesized from arachidonic acid.

  • Arachidonic acid is synthesized from linoleic acid, which is an essential fatty acid supplied from dietary lipids in adequate amounts.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e: p 213-215, 238-240.



Harper 30/e: p 213-215, 238-240.

questions.stem: A research team studying bacterial genetics exposes a culture to a chemical mutagen. The bacteria, which typically require minimal nutrition, are then plated on a nutrient-rich medium. Individual colonies that form are subsequently tested for their ability to grow on a minimal medium. Those failing to thrive are identified as mutants, and genomic sequencing reveals a deletion of a two-nucleotide segment in their DNA. What type of mutation does this deletion most likely produce?
questions.solutionHtml:
g>often results in a truncated protein.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B. Conservative mutation (Incorrect): It is a Missense mutation which leads to the substitution of a given amino acid with a chemically similar amino acid.

 

Option C. Missense mutation (Incorrect): It leads to the replacement of a given amino acid with a different amino acid.

 

Option D. Nonsense mutation (Incorrect): It introduces a stop codon instead of a codon specific for an amino acid, causing premature chain termination.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The deletion of a two-nucleotide segment within a gene's coding region typically results in a frameshift mutation. Because the genetic code is read in triplets (codons), removing two nucleotides alters the reading frame downstream of the mutation, likely changing every subsequent amino acid in the protein product. This shift can lead to a nonfunctional protein due to extensive missense mutations and the potential introduction of a premature stop codon (nonsense mutation).

 

Ref: Harper 30/e:  p 417-418.



Harper 30/e: p 417-418.

questions.stem: Which of the following modifications is primarily responsible for the inactivation of genes found within CpG islands?
questions.solutionHtml:
:11pt;"> B. Phosphorylation: While phosphorylation is a crucial post-translational modification that affects protein function, it is not directly involved in the inactivation of genes within CpG islands.

 

Option C. Ubiquitination: Ubiquitination is a process that tags proteins for degradation and does not directly affect gene inactivation at the DNA level within CpG islands.

 

Option B. Acetylation: Acetylation, particularly of histone proteins, is generally associated with the activation of gene expression by making chromatin more accessible to transcriptional machinery, not inactivation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gene promoters and regulation by methylation and demethylation:

 

  • Majority of gene promoters have high CG content.

  • CpG islands are the most common sites of methylation-demethylation.

  • Thus, they play an important role in regulation of gene expression

  • CpG islands of promoters are typically unmethylated, which favours transcription.

 

Ref: DM Vasudevan 9/e: p 596

questions.stem: Following a positive ELISA screening test for HIV, a patient undergoes a confirmatory Western blot test. For this assay, which component is specifically separated using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis before being transferred to a membrane for detection?
questions.solutionHtml:
on:

 

Option A: Patient sera and Option B: Patient plasma: While these are used in the test, they are not separated by the gel. Instead, antibodies in the sera or plasma react with the HIV proteins on the membrane.

 

Option C: HIV RNA: This would not be used in a Western blot, which is a protein-detection method. HIV RNA could be detected using techniques like RT-PCR, not Western blot.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a Western blot test for HIV, the components that are separated using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and then transferred to a membrane for detection are HIV proteins. These proteins are detected by their reaction with antibodies in the patient's serum, confirming the presence of an HIV infection.

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9/e: 736.

The affected cells exhibit defective DNA synthesis, characterized by the production of numerous short DNA fragments, each with RNA sequences at their 5' ends. This observation suggests a failure in a critical step of the DNA replication process. Which gene, essential for DNA replication and repair, is most likely affected by this mutation?

Option B: DNA helicase (Incorrect): They bind to the single-stranded DNA near the replication fork → separates the double strands and keeps them apart. Its deficiency would result in no DNA synthesis.

 

Option C: DNA ligase (Incorrect): If it is defective, it causes accumulation of short pieces consists only of DNA, because this enzyme functions once after the removal of RNA primer.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old baby has developmental delay, and the blood work shows megaloblastic anaemia, though B12 and folate are in the higher range. Urinalysis shows formation of a crystalline substance upon standing. Supplementation of the child’s diet with uridine reversed all the clinical symptoms. The crystalline substance is composed of which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Orotate

 

The child is diagnosed to have hereditary orotic aciduria, which is due to a mutation in UMP synthase → leads to orotic acid accumulation in the urine.

 

On treatment with uridine, the block is bypassed and allows UTP, CTP and dTTP synthesis.

 

Uridine treatment has the beneficial effect of blocking.

 

Explanaton:

 

Option A. Uracil - While uracil is a pyrimidine base, the clinical scenario specifically points to the accumulation of orotate, a precursor in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, not uracil itself.

 

Option B. Thymine - Thymine is another pyrimidine base found in DNA, but the condition described does not lead to thymine accumulation.

 

Option D. Aspartate - Aspartate is an amino acid involved in various metabolic processes, including the urea cycle and nucleotide synthesis, but it is not the crystalline substance described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hereditary orotic aciduria, a rare autosomal recessive disorder, characterized by a deficiency in the enzyme UMP synthase, crucial for the de novo synthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides. The deficiency leads to an accumulation of orotic acid, which is excreted in the urine and can crystallize.

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9/e: p 587.

questions.stem: During a forensic investigation of a sexual assault case, the crime scene investigators have procured a semen sample and tissue samples from the victim. They have also obtained DNA samples from the victim and three suspects for analysis. To compare the variable number of tandem repeats (VNTR) among these samples, which technique is most suitable for the initial analysis?
questions.solutionHtml:
these regions.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. DNA sequencing: Though it can detect DNA similarities but It is expensive and time-consuming for forensic analysis. It can be used for a confirmatory analysis.

 

Option B. Northern blot: It is used to separate and detect RNA.

 

Option D. Western blot: It is used for detection of proteins.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Southern blot is the best technique for the initial analysis in this context, as it is used for DNA analysis, specifically to detect certain sequences within a DNA sample by using restriction enzymes and a DNA probe. This method is well-suited for VNTR analysis, which is a type of polymorphism that can be highly variable among individuals and is useful for forensic DNA typing.

These proteins come from the same mRNA transcript and gene but are differentially processed in different tissues.

     

    Option D. Upstream repression: This refers to a regulatory mechanism where gene expression is inhibited by factors binding to regions upstream of the gene. This mechanism does not explain the production of two different proteins from the same mRNA transcript as seen with Apo-B48 and Apo-B100.

In contrast, the liver cells do not perform this editing, resulting in the full-length Apo-B100 protein.

questions.stem: A research team is utilizing various laboratory techniques to quantify the concentration of DNA samples extracted from patient biopsies. They are considering the most appropriate method that would provide accurate, rapid, and non-destructive analysis. Which of the following instruments is best suited for the quantitative analysis of DNA in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>

 

Explanation:

 

A UV spectrometer (or spectrophotometer) is the standard and most widely used instrument for the rapid, non-destructive quantification of DNA.

 

DNA strongly absorbs ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 260 nm due to its nucleotide bases. Using Beer-Lambert’s law, the absorbance at this wavelength can be directly related to the DNA concentration:

 

This method is:

  • Fast
  • Non-destructive
  • Accurate for pure DNA samples.

 

In contrast to other methods, it does not require dyes, gels, or amplification, making it ideal for direct concentration measurement.

 

Other Options:

  • Option A. Gel electrophoresis:
    Useful for qualitative analysis (e.g., DNA size, integrity) but not as accurate for quantification. It is also destructive, and staining agents like ethidium bromide are needed.
  • Option C) Light microscope: Incorrect.
    A light microscope is used to visualize cells or large cell structures, not molecules like DNA, and cannot provide concentration data.
  • Option D) PCR machine: Incorrect.
    PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is designed to amplify specific DNA sequences, not for direct DNA quantification. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) can estimate copy numbers of specific targets, but not general DNA concentration before the amplification process.

 

Educational Objective (Polished):


DNA can be accurately quantified using UV spectrophotometry at 260 nm, exploiting the strong absorbance of nucleic acid bases. This method is non-destructive, fast, and reliable, and is widely used before downstream applications like PCR, cloning, or sequencing.

 

Ref: Vasudevan 9/e: 744.



Vasudevan 9/e: 744.

options.label: B

Diphtheria toxin targets and inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2), which is essential for the translocation step of protein synthesis on ribosomes. This inactivation prevents the movement of the ribosome along the mRNA, thus halting protein synthesis, which can lead to cell death.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman who has inherited one mutant allele of the BRCA1 gene has a 60% risk of developing breast cancer by age 50. The BRCA1 gene encodes a protein that plays a crucial role in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks. Which DNA repair process is most likely impaired by a deficiency in BRCA1 protein function?

protein would affect the event of homologous recombination.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Removal of thymine dimers: This is generally managed by nucleotide excision repair, not by homologous recombination.

 

Option B. Removal of RNA primers: RNA primers are removed during DNA replication, a process unrelated to the repair function of BRCA1.

 

Option C. Removal of carcinogen adducts: Like thymine dimers, carcinogen adducts are typically addressed by nucleotide excision repair.

 

Educational Objective:

 

BRCA1 protein is fundamentally involved in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks primarily through homologous recombination, a critical process during cell division that ensures the accurate repair of DNA to prevent mutations that could lead to cancer. When BRCA1 function is compromised, the efficiency of homologous recombination repair is significantly reduced, which increases the risk of genomic instability and contributes to cancer predisposition, particularly breast and ovarian cancers.

Educational Objective:

 

Sickle cell anemia is caused by a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene, which leads to the replacement of glutamic acid with valine at the sixth position of the β-globin chain. This single amino acid change results in the production of hemoglobin S (HbS), which polymerizes under low-oxygen conditions, causing the red blood cells to take on a sickle shape and leading to hemolytic anemia.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following options correctly lists the core histone proteins that make up the nucleosome?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) H2A, H2B, H3, H4    

    

Option B:                                           

 

  • Histones are a small family of closely related basic proteins.

  • H1 histones are least tightly bound to chromatin.

  • Nucleosomes (core histones) contain four major types of histones: H2A, H2B, H3, H4.

  • H3 and H4 form a tetramer containing two molecules of each (H3–H4)2, while H2A and H2B form dimers (H2A–H2B).

  • Under physiological conditions, these histone oligomers associate to form the histone octamer of the composition (H3–H4)2–(H2A–H2B)

 

Educational Objective:

 

The core histone proteins that constitute the nucleosome are H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e: p 371

questions.stem: In an experiment aimed at understanding DNA replication, a piece of radio-labeled DNA is allowed to undergo two rounds of replication within a non-radioactive medium. This setup is designed to track the distribution of the original radioactive material across the generations of DNA. Based on the known mechanism of semiconservative replication, what would be the expected outcome regarding the radioactivity of the DNA strands after two replication cycles?

options.label: A
options.text: All the strands will have radioactivity

options.label: C
options.text: Half of the DNA will have no radioactivity

options.label: D
options.text: Three–fourth of the DNA replicated will have radioactivity

questions.answerText: Half of the DNA will have no radioactivity
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-size:12.0pt;">Explanation:

 

DNA replication follows a semiconservative model, meaning that each daughter DNA molecule retains one original (parental) strand and synthesizes one new strand.

  • After the first round of replication, each of the two daughter DNA molecules contains one radioactive parental strand and one new non-radioactive strand. So, all DNA molecules are partially radioactive.

 

 

  • After the second round of replication, each of these hybrid molecules produces:
    • One hybrid DNA (still containing one radioactive strand)
    • One entirely new DNA molecule (both strands non-radioactive)

 

So now there are four DNA molecules total:

  • Two are hybrid (radioactive + non-radioactive)
  • Two are completely non-radioactive

 

Therefore, half of the DNA molecules (2 out of 4) are non-radioactive.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A: All strands will have radioactivity — Incorrect. Only the original strands are radioactive, and they are passed on to only half of the DNA molecules after two replications.

 

Option B: No strands will have radioactivity — Incorrect. The original radioactive strands still exist in two of the four DNA molecules.

 

Option D: Three-fourth of the DNA will have radioactivity — Incorrect. Only two out of four DNA molecules (i.e., 50%) retain radioactive material, not 75%.

 

Educational Objective:


Understand the implications of semiconservative DNA replication: in each new round, half of the DNA molecules retain part of the original strand. 

 

Ref: Harper 30/e page 381-387.

questions.stemHtml: A researcher at a genetics laboratory is analyzing a gel-based technique for DNA analysis. The process includes the separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis, transfer of the DNA from the gel to a nitrocellulose sheet, and identification using a labelled DNA probe. What is the molecular biology technique depicted in the image?
questions.solutionHtml:
he Southern (DNA), Northern (RNA), and Western (protein) blot transfer procedures.

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Southern Blotting - RNA: Laboratory technique used to detect a specific DNA sequence in the blood and tissue sample.

 

Option C: Northern Blotting - Protein: Molecular biology technique to study gene expression by detection of RNA in a sample.

 

Option D: Western Blotting -DNA Protein Interaction: Molecular biology technique to study individual proteins in a sample.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The technique shown in the image is Southern Blotting, which is used for DNA detection. The process involves the separation of DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis, transfer of DNA onto a nitrocellulose or nylon membrane, and hybridization with a labelled DNA probe, which is then visualized through autoradiography. The presence of "32 P-labelled DNA probe" in the image confirms that the target for detection is DNA, not RNA or protein.

 

Ref: Harper 30/e page 456-457.
